clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive early-childhood neurodegeneration combining a severe sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy with progressive central nervous system involvement
Caused by biallelic mutations in GAN encoding gigaxonin, which regulates the turnover of intermediate filaments
Tightly curled, kinky hair that differs from the parents' is a characteristic and useful clinical clue
The neuropathy causes distal weakness, sensory loss, areflexia and gait difficulty, with later ataxia, nystagmus, pyramidal signs and cognitive decline
The pathological hallmark is giant axons distended by disorganised accumulations of neurofilaments, seen on nerve biopsy
MRI often shows cerebral and cerebellar white-matter abnormalities reflecting central involvement
The intermediate-filament disorganisation is generalised, so other filament-containing tissues (including hair) are affected
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, addressing mobility, contractures, respiratory function and nutrition
reference.pathophysiology: Giant axonal neuropathy is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in GAN, encoding gigaxonin, an E3 ubiquitin-ligase adaptor that controls the degradation of intermediate filament proteins. Loss of gigaxonin leads to abnormal accumulation and disorganisation of neurofilaments within axons, producing the characteristic focal axonal swellings (giant axons) packed with densely aggregated neurofilaments. This intermediate-filament dysregulation is generalised, disrupting both peripheral and central axons and other filament-rich tissues such as hair, and drives progressive degeneration of the peripheral nerves, cerebellum, corticospinal tracts and cerebral white matter.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and other inherited sensorimotor neuropathies
Leukodystrophies with peripheral neuropathy (e.g. metachromatic leukodystrophy)
Other hereditary sensory and motor or motor neuropathies
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy in childhood
Mitochondrial disorders with combined central and peripheral involvement
Friedreich ataxia and other early-onset recessive ataxias with neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Targeted GAN genetic testing to confirm gigaxonin deficiency
Nerve conduction studies showing an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy
Nerve biopsy demonstrating giant axons with neurofilament accumulation
MRI brain assessing cerebral and cerebellar white-matter change
Examination and, if needed, microscopy of hair to document the characteristic kinky texture
Respiratory and swallowing assessment as disease advances
redFlags: Respiratory insufficiency from progressive neuromuscular weakness
Rapid neurological deterioration with new central signs
Severe scoliosis or contractures compromising function and respiration
reference.prognosis: Giant axonal neuropathy is progressive, with loss of ambulation typically in later childhood or adolescence and death often in the second or third decade from respiratory and bulbar complications; the course and severity vary with the underlying mutation.
pitfalls: Overlooking the characteristic kinky hair as a diagnostic pointer in a child with neuropathy
Attributing the picture to a purely peripheral neuropathy and missing the central involvement
Delaying nerve biopsy or genetic testing when the phenotype is suggestive
Neglecting respiratory and spinal surveillance that guide anticipatory care
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
